touches.text: Test tiers: commit, hourly, daily and weekly. Each tier runs only what it must, so a commit needs only its own proofs and the long runs wait for the long tiers; nothing runs just in case.

Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Every red and every orphaned file is fixed; one unrelated to the work in hand is ticketed, and once it is, that crossing can go ahead.
Trouble Ticket: an error that needs a non-automated fixer (CC or Akien).
The test before raising one: can only CC or Akien fix this? If not, it is a log line, not a trouble. One problem, one trouble.

A trouble ticket is a work order. Whoever fixed it reports the fix to the originator (the device or machine that raised it), and the originator marks it fixed. A trouble that comes back is not designed for yet; if recurrent problems appear, we'll explore that.
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).

A red is first a question: is the code wrong, or is the tooth measuring the wrong thing? An LLM reads the work against the component's why, the tooth's why and CP1-CP6, because even the Laws rest finally on the core principles. Either the code or the tooth changes, and a tooth change carries that decision in the same act (corrosion, 17.11.6). A tooth a hollow build could pass is worthless at every tier (Law 8).

The workflow drives it. When a step's work is finished, the ticket asks that step's gate. Once the gate passes, its post-gate probes send mail over the bus to every device that can do the next step, naming the step (BUILDME, PROVEME, ...), and a device comes to claim it. A builder never goes looking for what's next: it gets the mail and does that. When several compete, the least capable one that thinks it can do it claims it, leaving the more capable free for bigger work.

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf. WHY: encapsulation. The ticket crosses as a fileref and the other side builds its own instance, so nothing is shared across the boundary but the address.
Trouble tickets (3.4.3) live here. Any device has a direct line to raise one, not over the bus (2.3.7.1.3).

conflicts.text: The test before raising one: can only CC or Akien fix this? If not, it is a log line, not a trouble. One problem, one trouble.
conflicts.ticket_says: When the cast door refuses to create a ticket for a red, raise an unticketed trouble naming the door and the lacks. The trouble clears automatically when a later run tickets the red or the proof reads green.
conflicts.why: Outline 3.4.3.5 states: 'The test before raising one: can only CC or Akien fix this? If not, it is a log line, not a trouble.' The unticketed trouble may auto-clear without human intervention (if a later run succeeds or proof goes green), so it fails the test for being a trouble. It records a transient condition that may resolve itself, which is not 'something only CC or Akien can fix' in the present—it may need no fixing at all. The outline's principle is that troubles are work orders requiring human action, not records of potential issues that might self-resolve.
